base_properties.human_readable: NPT Article VI Reciprocal Disarmament Obligation (Binding Temporal Reading)

stakeholders.name: nnws_coalition
stakeholders.situation: Non-nuclear-weapon states acted in unison to foreswear nuclear weapons in exchange for a legally binding promise of disarmament from nuclear-weapon states. Under the reciprocal reading, they hold the moral and legal authority to demand compliance. Their power is collective—they can refuse to extend the treaty at review conferences, threaten withdrawal en masse, and demand verification protocols. But exit is constrained: withdrawal incurs security costs (loss of IAEA safeguards regime, isolation in the international community) and legal costs (treaty violation claims). They benefit from horizontal non-proliferation (the original coordination function) but are victimized by the indefinite modernization of NWS arsenals (breach of reciprocal obligation).

stakeholders.name: nws_strategic_autonomy
stakeholders.situation: Nuclear-weapon states retain the legal right to withdraw from the treaty (Article X) and the practical ability to ignore Article VI through reinterpretation as aspirational. The reciprocal reading imposes reputational and normative costs on modernization: each program must be justified as compatible with disarmament, which constrains the narrative space for force-posture changes. NWS interpret their obligation through the lens of security environment and deterrence stability, treating Article VI as a goal rather than a binding commitment. Their exit options (withdrawal, reinterpretation, de facto non-compliance) are higher-cost than NNWS exit but remain available, making them arbitrage-positioned rather than trapped. They are victimized by the reciprocal reading's assertion that modernization is unlawful, though they do not accept this interpretation.

stakeholders.name: nws_modernization_capability
stakeholders.situation: The military-industrial establishments, strategic commands, and defense ministries of NWS must justify force-posture changes within the narrative constraint imposed by Article VI: modernization programs are framed as 'maintaining credible deterrence while pursuing disarmament' rather than as indefinite arsenal expansion. This creates institutional friction. New weapons systems must receive rhetorical cover (arms control compatibility, deterrence stability justification). Testing regimes are constrained by Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty norms (even if not universally ratified). The institutional actors have constrained exit—they cannot simply abandon the disarmament narrative without provoking NNWS coalition responses—but possess more flexibility than NNWS due to NWS control of treaty interpretation.

stakeholders.name: verification_apparatus
stakeholders.situation: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) monitors NNWS compliance with non-proliferation obligations but has no mandate to verify NWS disarmament progress. Proposed bodies (International Atomic Energy Agency disarmament verification division, regional verification centers) are excluded from actual NWS arsenal monitoring. If present, these bodies would have institutional power to audit NWS declarations, constrain modernization narratives, and produce evidence of non-compliance. Their exclusion is the core structural injustice of the constraint: the verification asymmetry is not remediable unilaterally by the verification apparatus itself. They are trapped because their mandates depend on NWS consent, which is withheld.

stakeholders.name: npt_review_conferences
stakeholders.situation: Held every five years, these forums are where treaty interpretation is negotiated and contested. NNWS coalitions use review conferences to assert the reciprocal reading, propose verification protocols, and threaten non-extension (a move with real consequences: the treaty would lapse, eliminating the IAEA non-proliferation regime). NWS use the forums to defend the aspirational reading and block verification protocol adoption. Review conferences have real agenda-setting power (they can propose amendments, condition extensions, and establish new verification bodies) but enforcement power is limited—NWS can simply leave. The conferences are mobile-positioned because they operate within a framework (the treaty) but can shift the treaty's interpretation within limits.

stakeholders.name: ir_scholars_and_legal_experts
stakeholders.situation: International relations scholars, legal experts, and think-tank analysts produce interpretive discourse legitimating the three readings. They do not enforce the treaty but shape the normative framework within which enforcement is contested. Legal opinions on whether Article VI is binding are produced by scholars and advisory bodies; these opinions are cited by both NNWS coalitions and NWS in their disputes. The analytical seat is neutral: they document the readings and their structural implications without being positioned as winners or losers.

stakeholders.name: potential_proliferators
stakeholders.situation: States tempted to develop nuclear weapons (Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, etc.) face a bargain whose credibility depends on the reading's status. The reciprocal reading strengthens the argument that NNWS have legitimately forsworn the option in exchange for binding NWS disarmament commitment, which increases moral and political pressure against proliferation. If the reciprocal reading gains traction and verification is implemented, the bargain's credibility rises and proliferation pressure is reduced. But if the reciprocal reading erodes (NWS modernize without disarmament progress), the bargain's credibility degrades and potential proliferators can claim they are victims of a non-reciprocal arrangement. Potential proliferators benefit from a strong reciprocal reading (it enforces the bargain and makes proliferation less attractive) but are disadvantaged when NWS appear to indefinitely retain arsenals without reciprocal constraint.

six_questions.coordination_function: The treaty coordinates global non-proliferation: all states pledge to prevent horizontal proliferation (NNWS foreswear nuclear weapons; NWS forgo assistance to NNWS developers) in exchange for NNWS gaining civilian nuclear technology access and NWS committing to disarmament. The reciprocal reading asserts that disarmament is not optional contingency but the coordination's essential quid-pro-quo centerpiece—NNWS cannot be asked to surrender the nuclear option permanently unless NWS are also surrendering their arsenals under binding timeline.
six_questions.transfer_function: NNWS permanently transfer the strategic option (right to develop independent nuclear arsenals) to the global security regime. In exchange, NWS are supposed to transfer binding commitment to pursue disarmament with measurable temporal progress toward complete nuclear elimination. Under the reciprocal reading, this is a genuine reciprocal exchange: permanent constraint-on-development in exchange for binding constraint-on-NWS-strategy. Under the oligopoly reading (sibling), NNWS transfer the option with only aspirational reciprocation from NWS—an asymmetric transfer, not a bargain.
six_questions.absent_voices: States that withdrew from the treaty (North Korea, 2003) and states that developed nuclear arsenals outside the regime (India, Pakistan, Israel) are absent from the formal NPT review process but present in the background as evidence of legitimacy erosion. They argue that the treaty's non-reciprocal structure—NNWS foreswear permanently while NWS retain indefinite arsenals—invalidates the bargain. Their absence from NPT forums is structured: the treaty's enforcement regime does not include them, so their objections cannot be directly addressed. Revolutionary governments (Iran under various political conditions) are also intermittently absent or withdrawn, making the bargain's credibility contested.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If the reciprocal disarmament reading were to completely vanish from international discourse—if Article VI were globally accepted as purely aspirational without any binding temporal requirement—the global nuclear order would rearrange. NNWS coalitions would fracture: some would extend the treaty indefinitely as a non-proliferation mechanism alone; others would withdraw to pursue independent deterrents or abandon the regime. The institutional framework for managing horizontal non-proliferation (IAEA safeguards, export controls, supply-side verification) would persist, but the legitimacy of NWS monopoly would erode. Proliferation pressure would rise. Conversely, if the reciprocal reading became universally binding and verified (Article VI timelines enforced, NWS on measurable disarmament schedules), the nuclear order would reorganize entirely: NWS arsenals would contract, verification regimes would expand, and the treaty would become a genuine reciprocal constraint rather than a horizontal non-proliferation mechanism with NWS exemption.
six_questions.founding_problem: The founding problem (1968-1970 negotiation period) was horizontal proliferation: multiple states were pursuing independent nuclear arsenals (France, China, many others were suspected), creating a multipolar nuclear world with instability and crisis risks. The NPT was negotiated to freeze the nuclear club at the five permanent UNSC members and prevent proliferation among the rest. The original purpose was to preserve the NWS monopoly while offering NNWS reassurance through two mechanisms: (1) civilian nuclear technology access (Atoms for Peace), and (2) Article VI disarmament commitment. The founding bargain traded NNWS foreswear for NWS disarmament; this is the reciprocal reading's grounding.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Nonproliferation scholars and IAEA historical data confirm that the NPT has been effective at reducing the rate of proliferation relative to the pre-1970 trajectory: if the trend had continued, 20-30 nuclear-armed states would exist by 2026; instead, nine do (five signatories, four non-signatories). The founding problem of multipolar proliferation has been substantially addressed. However, the question of whether the bargain remains reciprocal is contested. NNWS delegations at NPT Review Conferences (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020) and legal scholars from non-NWS backgrounds attest that the founding problem's solution has been made contingent on Article VI compliance—that is, the trade ceases to hold if NWS indefinitely modernize arsenals without reciprocal disarmament. NWS governments and their legal advisors assert that good faith is being pursued 'in good faith' (their reading), pointing to bilateral arms control agreements (START, New START) as evidence. However, international law scholars and NNWS coalitions outside the beneficiary set attest that these agreements often redistribute warheads rather than reduce arsenals, and that no binding timeline for complete disarmament exists. The statement 'the reciprocal bargain is being fulfilled in good faith' comes exclusively from NWS; no corroborating source outside the NWS beneficiary set validates this claim.

omegas.question: Is Article VI a binding legal obligation with measurable temporal requirements, or an aspirational commitment whose fulfillment is contingent on security environment?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Authoritative legal interpretation by the International Court of Justice via advisory opinion on NPT Article VI obligations, or universal acceptance of a binding verification protocol with timelines by all NPT states. Until such resolution, the reading remains contested.
omegas.impact: If Article VI is binding and temporal: NWS modernization becomes unauthorized under international law, NNWS coalition gains normative and legal leverage for remedies, and the constraint reclassifies from snare (NWS capturing the treaty) to genuine tangled_rope (real reciprocity with enforcement asymmetry). If Article VI remains aspirational: the constraint reverts to snare classification, NNWS forfeiture becomes permanent and irrevocable, and the treaty becomes a mechanism for locking in horizontal non-proliferation without reciprocal NWS constraint.
omegas.description: Whether Article VI carries binding legal force or remains hortatory aspiration — the core kernel contest.

omegas.question: Is the absence of Article VI verification mechanisms an intentional NWS design choice (to preserve strategic autonomy) or an implementation gap that should be filled?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Historical record of negotiation (declassified documents) and NNWS insistence at review conferences. If NWS deliberately excluded verification to preserve autonomy, the gap is structural extraction. If the gap is portrayed as accidental or temporary, it becomes remediable through protocol negotiation.
omegas.impact: If the verification gap is intentional design: the constraint becomes pure extraction (NWS capture of the treaty apparatus). If remediable: the gap is a structural injustice that, once filled, would enforce the reciprocal reading and constrain NWS modernization. This determines whether the NNWS have a plausible legal remedy or must accept permanent asymmetry.
omegas.description: Whether verification absence is deliberate capture or remediable oversight — determines remediation pathway.

omegas.question: As NWS modernize their arsenals over time without measurable disarmament progress, does the reciprocal bargain lose credibility such that NNWS withdrawal rates should rise?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Longitudinal analysis of NNWS NPT extension voting patterns, withdrawal threats, and stated rationales at review conferences. If credibility erosion is occurring, NNWS coalition should become more fragmented and conditional on Article VI compliance signals.
omegas.impact: If erosion is occurring: the reciprocal reading becomes increasingly contested and NNWS pressure for verification or disarmament acceleration will intensify. The constraint's temporal horizon shortens (NNWS coalitions set extension deadlines conditioned on verification). If credibility is stable: the reciprocal reading remains a live claim but with limited enforcement leverage against NWS modernization.
omegas.description: Whether the reciprocal bargain is eroding under the weight of NWS non-compliance.

omegas.question: This constraint instantiates ONE reading of the contested NPT Article VI kernel. Two sibling readings (oligopoly_enforcement_reading, withdrawal_sovereignty_reading) produce different structural classes, different victim sets, and different enforcement mechanisms from the same treaty text. What empirical or conceptual resolution would privilege one reading over the others as the treaty's 'true' obligation?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: No single empirical fact can resolve this. The three readings reflect different committer framings (NNWS coalition vs. NWS strategic doctrine vs. sovereigntist interpretation). Resolution would require either: (a) universal acceptance of a binding interpretation protocol (all parties agree which reading is law), (b) International Court of Justice advisory opinion (legal authority), or (c) regime shift (new treaty supersedes or clarifies the NPT). Until such resolution, all three readings remain live.
omegas.impact: This reading asserts reciprocal disarmament as binding and temporal; if that assertion is incorrect, the entire classification chain is invalid. The engine computes the constraint's type from structural data; the competing readings would produce different data and different type assignments. The three-way contest is NOT disambiguated by a single metric or observation—it is a kernel-level ambiguity.
omegas.description: The kernel contest itself: which reading of Article VI is the treaty's true obligation? This reading vs. its siblings.

commentary.narrative_context: The Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (1970) enshrines a bargain: non-nuclear-weapon states foreswear independent nuclear arsenals; nuclear-weapon states agree to pursue disarmament in good faith. The reciprocal disarmament reading interprets Article VI as a binding legal obligation with temporal urgency, making NWS modernization a violation of treaty commitment. This reading stands against two sibling readings: the oligopoly enforcement reading (Article VI is aspirational; horizontal proliferation prevention is primary) and the withdrawal sovereignty reading (states may withdraw if security environment changes). The reciprocal reading shifts structural power: NNWS coalition gains normative leverage by asserting breach of contract; NWS strategic autonomy enters the victim set as modernization faces justification pressure; verification apparatus gains institutional salience as the enforcement mechanism's conspicuous absence. The constraint is CLAIMED as tangled_rope (genuine reciprocal coordination with asymmetric enforcement burden on the NWS modernization side) while authored metrics describe substantial suppression, rising theater, and real resistance from NWS powers. This gap is intentional and diagnostic: the engine measures whether the reading's structural data—beneficiaries (NNWS coalition, global stability), victims (NWS strategic autonomy)—align with classification or whether the reading's own logic produces a type divergence.
key_agents: nnws_coalition: Non-nuclear-weapon states acting through NPT review conferences and coalition diplomacy; organized power; claim Article VI is binding and temporally urgent.
nws_strategic_autonomy: Nuclear-weapon states' force-posture and modernization programs; powerful institutional actors; assert Article VI is aspirational and contingent on security environment.

verification_apparatus: IAEA and proposed nuclear disarmament verification bodies; structurally excluded from Article VI compliance monitoring; represent the institutional injustice of the constraint.
npt_review_conferences: Five-yearly forums where the interpretation contest plays out; agenda-setting power over treaty extension and protocol development.
ir_scholars_and_legal_experts: Analytical seat; produce the interpretive discourse that legitimates readings without being positioned as winners or losers.
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness measures the asymmetry between NNWS commitment (irrevocable) and NWS commitment (indefinitely aspirational under the oligopoly reading). The reciprocal reading asserts this asymmetry is a breach of contract and should be corrected, so extraction rises over time as NWS modernization continues without reciprocal disarmament progress (measured 0.48→0.62 over 56 years). Suppression measures the enforcement burden NNWS must shoulder: they cannot legally withdraw without reputational cost; their only leverage is coalition pressure and review-conference bloc voting. Rising suppression (0.52→0.71) reflects the NWS monopoly on exit: they can withdraw from the treaty or simply ignore Article VI, while NNWS face institutional and security costs for withdrawal. Theater ratio measures the performative fraction of NWS disarmament activity: bilateral arms control agreements (START, New START) are presented as disarmament but often involve warhead redistributions, not reductions in deployed arsenals. Rising theater (0.35→0.60) reflects increasing narrative management of modernization as compatible with disarmament commitment—the 'maintaining credible deterrence while pursuing disarmament' frame. Accessibility collapse is moderate-to-low (0.48) because alternatives to the treaty remain available, albeit with high political cost: NNWS can withdraw (like North Korea did) or proliferate (India, Pakistan, Israel did), though doing so incurs isolation. Resistance is high (0.74) because NNWS coalitions actively push back at review conferences and through legal argumentation. The measurement series track the interval from NPT entry-into-force (1970) to present (2026), with projections to 2030 (the next likely review conference deadline and competition-timeline constraint endpoint).
commentary.directionality_logic: NNWS beneficiaries derive d near 0.1–0.2 (beneficiaries + constrained exit): they gain security through horizontal non-proliferation but pay through forswearing independent capability; exit is constrained by institutional and security costs. NWS strategic autonomy derives d near 0.85–0.95 (victims + arbitrage exit): they pay through the binding reading's constraints on modernization justification but retain legal and practical exit via withdrawal. The payer sides (nws_strategic_autonomy and nws_modernization_capability) are differentiated because one is strategic choice (NWS can exit or ignore Article VI) and the other is institutional practice (military establishments must justify programs through disarmament-compatible framing, which is a real constraint even if legally unenforceable). This differentiation explains why the same institutional actor (NWS) experiences different d values: strategic autonomy sits at the full-target end of d; modernization capability sits near moderate-target (constrained but not trapped).
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the NNWS coalition seat, Article VI is a binding legal obligation whose violation by NWS modernization is grounds for remedy (treaty renegotiation, verification protocol, enforcement mechanism). From the NWS seat, Article VI is a good-faith aspirational commitment shaped by security contingency; modernization is necessary to maintain credible deterrence (presented as supporting disarmament by preventing proliferation pressure). The engine computes these as different constraint types: from the NNWS seat, this is tangled_rope (real coordination function, asymmetric extraction, active enforcement burden on NNWS side); from the NWS seat, this is rope (genuine coordination with acceptable overhead from both sides). The computed divergence MEASURES the interpretive contest: where the seats agree on structure, both compute the same type; where they diverge (which should be here), the divergence is the evidence that the reading is contested.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem (horizontal proliferation of independent nuclear arsenals) has been substantially solved by the NPT's effectiveness at preventing proliferation relative to the 1960s trajectory. Under the oligopoly reading, the treaty continues to serve its function (preventing new entrants) and mandatrophy does not apply. Under the reciprocal reading, the mandate has partially atrophied: the original purpose was to trade horizontal non-proliferation for NWS commitment to eventual disarmament, but NWS have indefinitely postponed disarmament while maintaining the NNWS foreswear. The theater ratio rising to 0.60 by 2026 reflects this atrophy: NWS disarmament activity is increasingly performative (treaty rhetoric without measurable arsenal reduction). The constraint persists not because the original problem requires it (proliferation is suppressed) but because NWS benefit from the lock-in (NNWS remain non-nuclear while NWS retain their arsenals). The reciprocal reading names this as mandate erosion and calls for remediation (Article VI verification, binding timelines). The oligopoly reading does not call for remediation because it never made the original mandate temporal or binding.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint is the reciprocal disarmament reading of the contested NPT Article VI kernel (kernel_id: npt_treaty_1970). The kernel is Article VI's text: 'Each of the Parties undertakes to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.' The reading contest centers on whether 'in good faith' and 'early date' impose binding legal obligations with measurable timelines, or are aspirational goals contingent on security environment. The reciprocal reading asserts binding obligation and temporal urgency. The oligopoly enforcement reading asserts Article VI is aspirational; horizontal proliferation prevention (Articles I-II) is the primary binding obligation. The withdrawal sovereignty reading asserts Article X (withdrawal right) is the primary obligation, superseding Article VI when security environment changes. Each reading produces a different ε, different beneficiary/victim structure, different type classification, and different enforcement mechanism. This constraint (reciprocal_disarmament_reading) should be linked via network.affects_constraints to the sibling readings once they are authored.

network.dual_formulation_note: The NPT Article VI kernel contest produces three structurally distinct constraints. Each reading instantiates different ε, different beneficiary/victim structures, and different type classifications from the same treaty text. The reciprocal_disarmament_reading asserts Article VI is binding temporal obligation; oligopoly_enforcement_reading asserts Article VI is aspirational with Articles I-II primary; withdrawal_sovereignty_reading asserts Article X withdrawal right is primary and supersedes Article VI. These three constraints are linked by network.affects_constraints; they form a constraint family where the contest among readings is the primary structural fact. Each reading's omega variables should document the interdependencies: if one reading is falsified by legal interpretation or state practice, it affects the credibility of the others.
